sports.description: Sergi Solans (22) celebrates after notching his third MLS brace and 14th goal of his rookie season. | Real Salt Lake Real Salt Lake secured a 2-1 victory and a spot in the MLS Playoffs in the high-stakes, must-win Decision Day matchup against the LA Galaxy in front of a roaring crowd of 20,738 fans at America First Field. Solans and Booth lift RSL to playoff berth Spanish sensation Sergi Solans continued his impressive rookie MLS campaign, netting his 15th goal in the 10th minute to give RSL the early lead, putting him just two goals shy of the MLS rookie regular season scoring record of 17 goals (Cyle Larin in 2015 with Orlando City SC). The scoring continued with Utah native Zach Booth netting his second goal of the 2026 season just two minutes later. With the Decision Day victory, Real Salt Lake has officially punched its ticket to the postseason for a sixth consecutive season, the longest active playoff streak in the Western Conference. Although the evening was a nail biter the home side further cemented itself as a constant within the best squads in the Western Conference, earning ninth place and a spot in the Wild Card match. Quotable “We could only do what we could, which was win the game and then the universe had to do its thing, it’s gotta cook. We were in the right spot to receive its blessings and all we talked about was controlling what we can, and tonight the guys did a great job.“ — RSL coach Pablo Mastroeni Game summary The Claret-and-Cobalt opened up the Decision Day battle with energy, pushing up the pitch immediately as Solans and Canadian defender Luc de Fougerolles each earned tangible scoring opportunities in the second and fifth minutes. Although the early momentum continued with the home side netting two goals within minutes of each other, the LA Galaxy found the back of the net in the 40th minute to make the score 2-1. sports.title: “I’m so tired”: Matheus Cunha dismayed by Man United’s weak mentality that cost them a win vs Aston Villa
sports.description: “I’m so tired”: Matheus Cunha dismayed by Man United’s weak mentality that cost them a win vs Aston Villa Manchester United came back from two goals down in each half to eventually clinch a point after a thrilling tie against Aston Villa on Sunday. The visitors scored twice within the first five minutes of the first half and then scored another two within the opening eight minutes of the restart. On both occasions, the Red Devils managed to claw their way back, with Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans scoring in the first 45 minutes before substitutes Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu combined in added time to ensure the game finished 4-4. Will it be enough for Michael Carrick to remain at the helm? Only time will tell, but as most fans inside Old Trafford saw, the mistakes of key players let him down once again. Matheus Cunha cannot believe the weak mentality on show Diogo Dalot was at fault for two of those goals, and how the Portuguese defender has remained at the club for so long is beyond puzzling at this point. Matheus Cunha, who won the first penalty, was candid in his assessment after the game, revealing that he was tired of the way the team performed tonight. United only seemed to wake up after conceding and not from the start, and that mentality needs to change immediately, as this style of play is simply unsustainable. “I’m so tired and also disappointed. After the other night we talked about how we concede goals and have the mentality to come back in the game. Time for major changes “We did it again where we had to play like Manchester United and go forward. We showed courage but we only do this after we concede goals: showed character after conceding goals. “If we had shown that character and courage before then we will win more games. I don’t know why we are making it hard for ourselves. “We all work hard and we all want to be the best. We need to change our mentality from the beginning.” No wonder everyone wanted INEOS to strengthen the backline in the summer. Hopefully, they finally heed the call in January. sports.title: Cowboys Scheme Leaves Defensive Backs Blind To Ball
sports.description: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images The Dallas Cowboys secondary has gone months without a single interception by a defensive back. The unit features high-priced players and a deep roster. On Nov. 17, 2025, safety Markquese Bell secured the last interception by a Cowboys safety. That date feels like ancient history in a season that has already slipped away. The only three picks the team has this year belong to linebackers Shemar James, DeMarvion Overshown, and Dee Winters. Defensive coordinator Christian Parker told Yahoo Sports exactly why the corners and safeties are stuck in neutral. He said, “I think that just has to do with No. 1 you’re dictating coverage so you can find the ball.” Parker admitted the scheme forces defensive backs into man-to-man coverage where they cannot see the quarterback’s eyes. He added, “I mean, I think it’s as simple as that.” The team tries to use match-zone coverage, but the execution keeps them from finding the ball in the air. The Cost of Man Coverage When you force corners to play tight man coverage, you give up yards. Cornerback DaRon Bland leads the team with six pass breakups, but he has also allowed an NFL-high 438 yards. Quarterbacks have thrown for three touchdowns against him with a rating of 117.4. Parker acknowledged the issue directly. “Yeah, and we need more from him,” Parker said. He noted that Bland has been close on many contested catches but needs to finish the plays. The problem is that one mistake in the secondary puts the whole defense in the spotlight. If the linebackers are supposed to have the vision, why are the defensive backs getting burned? Parker said the linebackers play with more vision because they are in zone. Meanwhile, the corners and safeties are locked in man coverage. This leaves them blind to the quarterback’s progressions until it is too late. A Drought That Hurts the Season The Cowboys are sitting at 3-5 after losing to the Arizona Cardinals in overtime on Sunday, Nov. 1. The loss came after the team let a 24-10 lead slip away in the fourth quarter. Dak Prescott never threw a pass on the final drive after an onside kick recovery. He took a sack and watched Javonte Williams run for three yards on third-and-16. Prescott said, “Maybe the drive after the onside kick,” and called it the turning point. But the defense cannot help the offense if they cannot take the ball away. Defensive lineman Quinnen Williams called out the unit for their lack of execution. “We’re the problem. We’re the reason why we’re losing these games,” he said. Dallas opponents succeed on 51.4% of their third-down attempts. The Colts, who Dallas faces on Sunday, Nov. 8, will exploit this weakness. If the scheme does not change, the secondary will continue to give up big plays.

sports.title: Jason Kelce breaks down ‘really important’ Chiefs vs Jets moment Justin Fields got wrong
sports.description: Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images Justin Fields saw rare action for the Kansas City Chiefs. It did not go as planned. Former New York Jets quarterback Justin Fields has been patiently waiting for a chance. And when you are sitting behind Patrick Mahomes, that does not happen very often. The Chiefs drew up a play for Fields against his former team, bringing him in to attempt a quarterback sneak. Unfortunately he failed to execute, with the Jets stopping him short and recovering the ball for a fumble. Jason Kelce gives verdict on Justin Fields fumble A key factor for any quarterback entering the game is his chemistry with his offensive line. And this was part of where it all went wrong. Former NFL star Jason Kelce pointed to the snap from Chiefs center Creed Humphrey, noting that this started the play badly. Kelce wrote on X : “Center QB exchange is really important for QB sneak, and often overlooked. Because of the way the Center fires off the ball, the Quarterback, or whoever is taking the snap needs to get reps full speed of the snap from the center in practice to get an accurate feel.” But this does not absolve Fields from blame. Kelce noted that the backup quarterback may have got his timing all wrong. “There’s also a timing to it from the QB, not sure how many Fields has done, but he looked like he moved quickly before securing the snap there. “I like that KC is finally running it, but an unfortunate start. There’s more nuance to that play than people realize.” In the opening eight weeks of the NFL season, Justin Fields did not take a single snap. And he really needed to make this one count. A fan wrote on X: “The QB sneak/tush push with Justin Fields went so well I expect Andy Reid won’t call it again for the rest of his life.” There will be plenty for Reid and his staff to analyze on this play in the film room on Monday. Fields will just need to pray that he gets another chance. sports.title: Briscoe Takes Pole As Homestead Finale Sets Stage For Title Showdown
sports.description: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images Chase Briscoe secured the pole position for the NASCAR Cup Series season finale, putting Joe Gibbs Racing ahead before the green flag drops on Sunday. The No. 19 Toyota driver posted a lap of 166.687 mph to edge his teammate Denny Hamlin by a razor-thin 0.017 seconds, per Motorsport.com NASCAR Cup. The result follows a year in which the team often struggled in qualifying, and Briscoe secured the win at a crucial moment. The 267-lap race at Homestead-Miami Speedway will decide the 2026 champion, and starting from the front row is the best possible spot to control the pace. A Tight Pack for the Title Three drivers remain in the championship battle, and their starting spots are closely grouped. According to Motorsport.com NASCAR Cup, Kyle Larson, who leads the points, will start fourth and requires only eight stage points to secure his third title. His closest rival, Christopher Bell, qualified sixth and trails by 67 points. Denny Hamlin is second on the front row but faces a steep climb, 70 points behind Larson with 76 points available in the race. Briscoe, who is out of title contention, stated “Yeah, our car was really good yesterday in practice too,” when discussing the speed his team found on Friday. Hamlin admitted he lost the pole by “trying to save the tires a little bit too much coming to the green,” which cost him the top spot by a fraction of a second. Brad Keselowski’s Final Bow The starting grid also marks a sad end for Brad Keselowski in his final race as a driver and co-owner for RFK Racing. Keselowski lost control of his car at the exit of Turn 4 during qualifying and spun into the inside wall, leaving him starting in the 40th and final position. “The track’s really, really slick,” said Keselowski afterward, explaining the difficult conditions that led to his crash. He added that he “Was trying to find a place that had some grip” but simply could not find it, noting, “Wish i could have that one back, but just trying to find something to be as fast as i could be.” His misfortune highlights the unforgiving nature of the 1.5-mile oval where grip is scarce. sports.title: Bears Must Target Cornerback Riq Woolen Over Chase Young
sports.description: Eric Hartline-Imagn Images The Chicago Bears face a critical choice before the trade deadline. While chatter swirls around a potential reunion with Khalil Mack or a move for Chase Young, the real need lies in the secondary. Due to a thumb injury sustained during the Week 8 victory, the team has just placed running back Zavier Scott on injured reserve. Scott will miss at least four games, leaving the depth chart thin. The current roster cannot afford to ignore the pass coverage holes. Why the Secondary Takes Priority Many fans want a big edge rusher to help the pass rush. However, league evaluators have shifted their view on what the team actually lacks. On Wednesday, ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler reported that the Bears have been linked to edge-rushers such as Khalil Mack, but a few league evaluators told him that cornerback is becoming more of a need. Adding another pass-rusher does not fix the leaks in the coverage unit. The offense has been strong, rushing for 1,206 yards through eight games. The defense must match that energy to keep Caleb Williams off the field. The Case for Woolen Over Young Reports indicate the Bears have checked in on Saints defensive end Chase Young. The NFL Rumors X account shared that the Bears and 49ers have checked in on the Saints’ Chase Young. While Young has stats to back him up, he is not the right fit for this specific roster gap. The team is also in deep competition with the Lions to acquire Riq Woolen from the Eagles. Thomas R. Petersen reported via X on Thursday that they are reportedly in deep competition with Lions to acquire Riq Woolen from the Eagles. Woolen offers a one-year solution that fits the cap and the timeline. science.title: Legendary sci-fi magazine 'Starlog' returns as a yearly release, just in time for its 50th anniversary
science.description: null "Starlog" was one of the greatest sci-fi and fantasy magazines ever, and after a 17-year absence, it's being resurrected. The legendary sci-fi mag went dark back in 2009 as part of the wave of popular publications folding due to years of declining readership and subscriptions. But as of Nov. 13, this geek favorite periodical returns as an annual print edition, and it's available for pre-order now. It’s another indication of digital fatigue in the world, and fans of a certain age will recall the pleasure of poring over each colorful issue packed with in-depth interviews, behind-the-scenes photos, TV guides, classic movie retrospectives, book reviews, con news, and VFX features. The triumphant relaunch of "Starlog" magazine happens on Nov. 13, 2026 (Image credit: Fangoria Holdings) "Starlog" launched in 1976, in the pre-" Star Wars " days, under the leadership of editor-in-chief Terry O’Quinn. It first arrived with artist Jack Thurston's beautiful painted "Star Trek" cover, featuring William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk and Leonard Nimoy’s Spock, set against the U.S.S. Enterprise near a shimmering black hole. The magazine continued to inform the science fiction community about upcoming sci-fi TV shows and blockbuster Hollywood films for over three decades; I fondly recall reading each informative and entertaining monthly issue cover-to-cover. Just in time to honor its 50th anniversary this year, "Starlog" blasts back into the sci-fi universe with Issue #375 showcasing cover artwork created by Armenian artist Gabriel Yeganyan. Its geek culture legacy, covering iconic franchises like "Star Wars," "Star Trek," and "Alien," will now live on thanks to Fangoria Holdings and io9 co-founder Annalee Newitz, editor-in-chief. Three vintage "Starlog" magazine issues from my personal collection! (Image credit: Jeff Spry) "During its original 33-year run, 'Starlog' documented science fiction as it evolved across film, television, books, technology, and culture," said 'Fangoria's Tara Ansley. "Fifty years after the magazine first launched, the line between science fiction and the real world has become increasingly difficult to separate. That makes this an especially interesting time to bring 'Starlog' back. Technology may change, but the most compelling questions have always been about people: how we live, what we create, and what kind of future we want to build." "Starlog" reloads for its first annual edition after a long hiatus on Nov. 13. You can pre-order the first issue (Issue 375 in continuity) on the Starlog website .

science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 8, 2005: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus
science.description: null On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express. Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years. During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole . It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes . Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras . These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere. Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this. It performed well, but eventually it stopped listening to commands. The spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere in January 2015. A Russian Soyuz rocket launches the Venus Express spacecraft to Venus on Nov. 8, 2005.. (Image credit: ESA) Why it mattered Venus Express established ESA as the third world organization to successfully send a probe to study Venus, following the United States and Soviet Union. (Japan's JAXA became the fourth five years later.) "By studying Venus, scientists learn how Earth-like planets change over time," reads a summary of the planet's exploration prepared by The Planetary Society. "Orbital studies [like Venus Express] hint that Venus may have hosted habitable oceans before becoming inhospitable." "By studying Venus, we can learn how Earth-like planets evolve and what shapes planets throughout the galaxy into temperate, lush worlds instead of sweltering hothouses. Venus also helps scientists model Earth’s climate, and may serve as a cautionary tale on how dramatically a planet’s climate can change," wrote the Society. An illustration of the Venus Express spacecraft in orbit around Venus. (Image credit: ESA) ESA returned to Venus in 2018 when BepiColombo, its joint mission with JAXA, used the planet's gravity to redirect its path toward the planet Mercury. Want more space history? science.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
science.description: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life. To aid in distinguishing between habitable and inhabited planets, planetary scientist Samantha Gilbert-Janizek of the University of California, Riverside, developed a model that simulates the evolution of a rocky planet without life. "The model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets," Gilbert-Janizek, who was a PhD student at the University of Washington when the research was conducted, said in a statement. Gilbert-Janizek built upon a model previously developed by Washington’s Rory Barnes that simulated the core, mantle, and crust of a planet. This new model pushed the simulation two steps further by incorporating the surface and atmosphere of the planet as well. In all, the model simulates 19 properties of a rocky planet that are not related to life, including the amount of heat a planet receives from its star , the exchange of heat and chemicals from the core to the surface, and the outflow of certain gases from the subsurface. Gilbert-Janizek’s starting point was to simulate the development of Earth had life never arisen here, therefore providing a baseline with which to compare to exoplanets . She ran the simulation from the birth of Earth 4.5 billion years ago to 500 million years into the future. The result was a lifeless world, but one that still had oceans and an atmosphere. "When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface," said Gilbert-Janizek. An illustration shows the landscape of a primordial Earth before life arose as lightning splits the skies (Image credit: Robert Lea (created with Canva)) What makes the simulation especially useful is its plug-and-play nature. Researchers can simply apply the bulk properties of whichever planet they are studying to the model, and then just let it run. If the result is a planet with an atmosphere that matches what is detected spectroscopically by the James Webb Space Telescope or, in the future, the various extremely large 30-meter-plus ground-based telescopes or NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory , then we know that planet probably does not have life as we know it. science.title: NASA Seeks Next Generation of Explorers to Join Astronaut Corps
science.description: NASA announced its 2025 Astronaut Candidate Class on Sept. 22, 2025, at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Credit: NASA/Helen Arase Vargas NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight. Applications are now open for the agency’s next class of astronauts, who will join NASA as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars. The next generation of astronauts will train to operate on the lunar surface, live and work beyond Earth, and take on missions that will push the boundaries of human exploration farther than ever before. U.S. citizens interested in joining the astronaut corps have until 11:59 p.m. EST Thursday, Dec. 3, to submit their completed application materials at: https://go.nasa.gov/3WyvlQi “This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars. Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage. NASA’s astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation. If you are ready to join that tradition, come help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure.” NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027 to begin training as the next class of astronaut candidates. “The window is open. The mission is waiting. And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson. The agency last opened applications in 2024. From more than 8,000 applications, 10 astronaut candidates were selected in 2025 and are currently completing nearly two years of training. “For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the Astronaut Selection Board at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. “It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space. The next generation of astronaut candidates could help write history while inspiring future scientists, engineers, and explorers.” Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates for its increasingly challenging missions. The agency has 32 astronauts active in the astronaut corps, and selected applicants will join their ranks to study spacewalking, lunar geology, operations of high-performance aircraft, and more. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before
science.description: null On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected. But a space maneuver accidentally exposed one of its batteries to the sun, and the spacecraft lost power. It fell silent forever in November 2006 . NASA launches the Mars Global Surveyor to Mars on a Delta II rocket on Nov. 7, 1996. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered As the first successful Mars mission since the two Viking launches in 1975, Mars Global Surveyor ushered in a new era of exploration of the Red Planet, not only through its own contributions to orbit-based science, but by serving a relay for surface-based rovers. As such, it became a primary pipeline for multiple concurrent Mars missions. "The [Mars Global Surveyor] mission overhauled scientists' understanding of Mars by studying the entire Martian surface, atmosphere and interior. Major findings included dramatic evidence that water still flows on Mars in short bursts down hillside gullies, and the identification of water-related mineral deposits leading to selection of a Mars rover landing site for a subsequent mission," read a NASA description of the probe. Mars Global Surveyor sent back more than 240,000 images to Earth during its nine active years. Want more space history? science.title: Send your name to Saturn's moon Titan with NASA's upcoming Dragonfly mission
science.description: null We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission. Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027. The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034. "Nearly a billion miles away, an extraordinary destination awaits. Titan has an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material," NASA officials wrote in the event page. "Upon arrival in 2034, Dragonfly will fly from place to place on this intriguing world to uncover clues about this remarkable moon, and the chemistry that could help us understand the ingredients for life." Dragonfly will be one of just a few flying crafts on another world, with the first being NASA's plucky Ingenuity mini-helicopter that arrived on Mars along with the still-running Perseverance rover in 2021. Ingenuity was only designed to make five flights, but made it to 72 until its blades were damaged during a landing on Jan. 18, 2024. NASA is now planning a SkyFall mission on Mars that would use three helicopters, and which may launch as soon as late 2028 for the Red Planet. Dragonfly, however, is not the first mission to Titan: that would be Huygens , which operated for just a few hours on Jan. 14, 2005 after deploying from the Cassini spacecraft. Huygens was the first lander on an outer solar system world, and measured Titan's atmosphere and took data from the surface. A mosaic image of Saturn's moon Titan composed of images produced by the Cassini spacecraft. (Image credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona/University of Idaho) For its part, Cassini flew by Titan more than 100 times before the mission concluded in September 2017 , providing valuable long-term data about the moon from above. Dragonfly aims to show the moon from up close for about 3.3 Earth years. Its destinations will include dunes and a young impact crater called Selk, according to NASA. "Dragonfly is expected to make one flight every one to two Titan days, which is called a Tsol and lasts about 16 Earth days," NASA officials added of the mission . Dragonfly will stop at a variety of geologic sites, where it will collect samples of surface material for analysis inside the rotorcraft by a suite of scientific instruments." science.title: Star Wars is experiencing a golden age of video games
science.description: After a tumultuous start to EA's rebooted Star Wars Battlefront series, in 2021 Lucasfilm and Disney decided to open up the development of new Star Wars games by bringing in different publishers and studios under the Lucasfilm Games banner. Now, over five years on, we can confidently say we're entering a new golden era of amazing Star Wars games . With LucasArts' successor calling the shots and coordinating a multitude of projects set in a galaxy far, far away, even EA's latest efforts like Squadrons and the Jedi series have taken bigger and bolder swings. Now, in 2026, the full potential of the Star Wars universe has become clearer with specific releases squarely aimed at niche audiences. It's become clear that future Star Wars games needn't be expensive endeavors full of familiar faces or concepts. Star Wars Zero Company and Galactic Racer 's restrained scope and confidence have been infectious, and, as it turns out, they're already recognized by all the parties involved as double-A success stories . Now this is podracing! The original Burnout studio, Criterion, would have been an excellent candidate, but instead they were sent to work in the Battlefield mines. Still, someone was interested in the idea, and the end result is glorious. Fast and furious, Star Wars: Galactic Racer ignores recent racing game trends and bets big on arcade-y vibes, uncomplicated controls, and a high skill ceiling that challenges you with extremely high speeds, tight turns, and unexpected interruptions as other drivers try to ruin your day. The not-so-secret sauce, however, was its runs-based structure, which injects the flexibility and replay value of roguelite games into the more traditional arcade racing structure that older gamers are familiar with. science.title: 'I think we will prevail': NASA chief Jared Isaacman on Artemis, China and the new moon race (exclusive)
science.description: null NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition. "I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com. We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program , and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. In fact, just prior to our conversation, it was announced that Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman will become the new deputy director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But the road from Artemis II's success to crewed lunar landings and, later, a permanent moon base will take a lot of launches of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) megarocket, Isaacman stressed. "You know, a lot of people, especially in the space community, start getting [into] if the landers are there or not. I don't really care about that right now. What I care about is that we are launching big rockets no less than once a year," he said. "I think that's imperative for NASA to be doing these deep-space human spaceflight missions right now," Isaacman added. "So, we had a great mission in April of '26. We will launch again in '27." That coming launch will be for Artemis III, a crewed mission to low Earth orbit that will test docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's private lunar landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon. "We need to continue to exercise those muscles," he said, referring to SLS liftoffs. "And, honestly, once a year isn't great, either. science.title: SpaceX launches mystery mission for US Space Force in gorgeous sunset liftoff from California (video, photos)
science.description: null SpaceX just launched a classified mission for the U.S. military. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base this evening (Nov. 6) at 7:48 p.m. EST (4:48 p.m. local California time; 0048 GMT on Nov. 7), rising into the sky as the sun sank toward the Pacific. The launch kicked off the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force , which we know little about. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force told us much about USSF-432 beforehand, and we learned tonight; SpaceX cut its webcast off about 10 minutes into the flight, shortly after the Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth for a landing. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base on Nov. 6, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) That touchdown occurred aboard the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange in the Pacific Ocean. It wrapped up the eighth flight for this particular booster, which is designated 1095. The Falcon 9's upper stage, meanwhile, continued carrying its mystery payload skyward. It could be headed to low Earth orbit , outside observers speculate. "It is possibly a batch of classified LEO satellites for the USSF's Space Based Sensing and Targeting (SBST) portfolio based on SpaceX's Starshield satellite bus, based on locations of rocket stage drop zones being exact fits with previous Starlink Group 15 launches," NextSpaceflight.com wrote in a mission description . Starlink is SpaceX's LEO broadband megaconstellation, which consists of more than 11,000 active satellites. Starshield is a similar system designed to provide services to the U.S. military and its allies. Starshield satellites are believed to be based heavily on the Starlink spacecraft bus. The Falcon 9's first stage after its landing on Nov. 6, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Previous Booster 1095 missions GPS-III 8 | 6 Starlink missions USSF-432 was the 119th Falcon 9 launch of 2026, and the 14th national-security flight of the rocket so far this year. The vast majority of Falcon 9 missions in 2026 — more than 70% — have been devoted to building out the Starlink megaconstellation. SpaceX has also launched six other missions this year. Three were operational flights of the company's Falcon Heavy rocket, while the other three were test missions of its next-gen Starship vehicle. SpaceX plans to retire both the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy shortly after the fully reusable Starship, the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, is up and running.

science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
science.description: null On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it. The Tycho supernova remnant as seen by the Chandra X-ray space telescope. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/RIKEN & GSFC/T. Sato et al; Optical: DSS) Why it mattered The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572 , is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star. While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky. "The 16th century exploding star, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia , was seen in daylight for about two weeks, and remained visible to the naked eye for 16 months," the University of California Berkeley wrote in 2004 . "Brahe's meticulous record of the brightening and dimming of the supernova now allows astronomers to identify its 'light signature" as that of a Type Ia supernova." "This was at the end of the Dark Ages in Europe, and these observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable," astronomer Alex Filippenko, who led a 2004 study on the origins of the Tycho supernova, said at the time . Today, astronomers are closely watching another star that might explode. Called T Corona Borealis , or the Blaze Star , the object is expected to be on the verge of exploding in a nova (a star explosion that is smaller than a supernova and may not destroy the star). is one of 11 known stars observed to have recurring nova explosions within gaps of 100 years or so.
